chapter: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
title: Benny Carter's studies, and Lennie Hayton's MGM sessions with a weak violinist
summary: Carter later studied arranging and violins in California. Horace sat in on Lennie Hayton's MGM soundtrack rehearsals and learned why Hayton used many violins to cover a studio executive's incompetent cousin.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Had Benny had some formal training in a sense in arranging or --

Oh, I think he did have some in Pittsburgh, but I know in his later years -- like right now and a few years back from the current year. Last time I talked to Benny, he had gone to school in California. I don't know to what institution -- to study arranging and to learn more about the violins because he made a lot of things for MGM for the
Yes, he was doing some TV things.

Yes, TV things, and it involved, you know, when you cut your sound tracks, like for 105 musicians, one of those things. I was fortunate enough to be in on some things that the great Russian composer and arranger, Lennie Hayton, Lynn Haven, you know, Lena Horne's husband -- I sat in on a lot of his sound tracks for MGM and the way he rehearsed the band, you know, and all, and I knew he was well versed in all those things. And that was the first time that I had seen a big band rehearse with the big sheets in front of them, and they didn't -- like, for instance, when we make an arrangement, we would have letter A, you know, letter B and C. Well, at the studios they'd have everything by numerals -- bar 74, bar 150, and, man, he could hear somebody make a bad note way down there even at 105, he'd stop the band and he would say, like, 12 violins, four of them playing first, four playing second, four playing third. And they would have maybe 16, you know, another playing fourth.

And I asked Lennie Benny one thing. This is very interesting. And this was -- with politics going on. I guess I can say this, but I says, 'Lennie, Benny,' I said, 'Why is it so necessary to have four first violins or, second four violins?' He says, 'You really want to know?' I said, 'Why, sure.' He says, 'Well, we've got a lot of politics here, and we have something in the

studios, what they call the blues and the greens, you know, those syndicates,|| you know, one of those things. And -- plus the fact that the number third -- the third number one violinist was so horrible. He was a cousin of some executive there, and this is how he gets in. And the other thing -- so you got to have that many deep to cover up the other guys because they sould like -- he says, "I'll show you what I mean sometime."

So one day he did -- not Ben then -- but he told me a lot of other things. So they were rehearsing something, and he stopped the band, and he looked at me, and I knew he was up to something. So he -- about 105 guys, you know -- Murray MacEachern McKeckny, you remember the trombone player?

I don't know if I pronounced it right. I know you know this guy. He's a great trombonist and alto saxophonist, great arranger -- he's made -- but he was in this particular band. Anyhow, he stopped the band, and he said, "Number three violin in the third chair, bar 84, go back a little bit and start playing it, bar 84, 85, 86, 87. Seems like something's wrong." This guy, nervous as he could be. Man, you could see perspiration coming on him because he wasn't -- he was a cousin of some executive there, and they

put him in, and, man, you should have heard him. He sounded like a high school kid, a beginner, you know. And Lennie Benny looked at me. He says, "Okay, fine. Now we can take it back from there." You know, he covered up good. But those are the things that happen. When he got to me it, he says, "You see now why we have to have that many deep?" I said, "Yes, I do."

So those things happen. You never know. The public doesn't know these things. They go to the theaters, and hear these sound tracks, if there's some trash, you know, behind the star and music interludes, you know, all that. But these are the things that happen, and it was real interesting to me, so that's that, you know, was
